narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The genre originated with 19th-century cattle farmers and minstrels (juglares) who traveled the Magdalena Grande region.
It evolved through the integration of the German-origin accordion with Indigenous flutes and African percussion.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Vallenato is traditionally performed in social settings like parrandas.
While the music is often for listening, it incorporates rhythmic footwork and body movement that reflects the syncopated nature of the four primary airs.
Watch for Piqueria improvisation.

Formation: Informal social space, often in close proximity to the musicians.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The core ensemble consists of the caja vallenata (a small hand-played drum), the guacharaca (a ribbed wooden stick scraped with a fork), and the three-line button accordion.
Listen for the Accordion, Caja vallenata, Guacharaca.
The pulse is 2/4 for son and paseo; 6/8 for merengue and puya..
A distinctive, bright, and often melancholic sound led by the accordion, underpinned by the dry, percussive scrape of the guacharaca and the steady, hand-played beat of the caja.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: La Gota Fría — Emiliano Zuleta/Carlos Vives; La Gota Fria — Carlos Vives (1993)

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Rafael Escalona, Emiliano Zuleta, Lorenzo Morales, Alejo Durán, and modern ambassadors like Carlos Vives.
Variants include the 'Nueva Ola' (New Wave) which fuses traditional sounds with pop, rock, and electronic elements.
A fusion of Spanish décima poetry, African rhythmic drumming, and Indigenous flute traditions.
